html:
Crystal planes in a cubic lattice
Controls act on
Plane family (Miller indices)
Guided tour
Drag in the figure to orbit: the teal sheet is a real 2D plane threading the lattice — seen edge-on it collapses to a line of atoms. The sheet is deep teal where it lies inside the cube and pale where it emerges past the faces. Atoms lying in the sheet keep their red colour but grow slightly and gain a teal rim.

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two identical cubic crystal lattices drawn side by side in perspective. Each is a three-by-three-by-three array of small red spheres standing for atoms, joined by thin black lines tracing the cube edges and the rows between nearest neighbors, so the block reads as open and transparent. In the left lattice, a translucent teal plane lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the middle sheet of atoms, appearing darker where it sits behind the front layer of spheres and paler where it emerges near the top face. In the right lattice, the highlighted plane is tilted instead, slicing diagonally from the lower left of the cube toward the upper right and intersecting a different set of spheres, its shading again splitting between a darker interior portion and a lighter one near the top. Holding the lattice fixed while changing only the orientation of the shaded plane makes that orientation the single variable in view. The pair conveys that one crystal holds many families of parallel atomic planes at differing angles and spacings, each able to produce its own X-ray diffraction.

elements: 27 small red spheres arranged as a 3x3x3 simple-cubic lattice (atoms), each with a dark red rim/specular highlight
thin black straight lines joining every pair of nearest-neighbour spheres along the three cube axes (3 sheets x 3 lines in each of x, y, z), forming the open wireframe grid
outer cube edges of the lattice, drawn slightly heavier than interior rows
one translucent teal plane cutting through the lattice, rendered double-sided
darker teal region of the plane where it lies behind the front layer of spheres, paler teal where it emerges past the top/side faces (depth-dependent shading)
the sub-set of red spheres that actually lie in the highlighted plane, drawn emphasised (slightly larger / brighter) so the learner sees which atoms the plane contains
Miller-index caption for the current plane family, e.g. (100), (110), (111)
interplanar spacing label d = a / sqrt(h^2+k^2+l^2) with its numeric value
faint ghost outlines of the other parallel planes of the same family, so the family reads as a stack

interactions.teaches: The teal sheet is a genuine 2D plane threading a 3D lattice, not a painted rectangle; rotating shows which atoms really lie in it and how the plane edge-on becomes a line of atoms.

interactions.label: Plane family (Miller indices)
interactions.teaches: One and the same crystal contains several families of parallel atomic planes at different angles; only the plane orientation changes while the red-sphere lattice stays fixed.

interactions.label: Which plane in the stack
interactions.teaches: Stepping to the next parallel plane of the family shifts the sheet by exactly the interplanar spacing d and highlights a different sheet of atoms — the d that enters Bragg's law.

interactions.label: Show whole parallel stack
interactions.teaches: The family is an evenly spaced stack: every atom in the crystal lies on some plane of the family, and the spacing shrinks as the Miller indices grow.

demo_steps.title: Left panel: planes parallel to a cube face
demo_steps.narration: The teal sheet lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the central sheet of nine atoms. This is the (100) family, spacing d = a.

demo_steps.title: Step to the neighbouring plane
demo_steps.narration: Sliding to the next plane translates the sheet by one lattice constant and lights up the front layer of atoms instead — successive planes of the same family are separated by d.

demo_steps.title: The whole (100) stack
demo_steps.narration: Showing all three planes at once reveals that every atom in the crystal belongs to one plane of this evenly spaced family.

demo_steps.title: Right panel: diagonal (110) planes
demo_steps.narration: Now the same lattice is cut diagonally from the lower left toward the upper right. A different set of spheres lies in the plane, and the spacing tightens to d = a/√2.

demo_steps.title: A steeper family still
demo_steps.narration: The (111) planes slice across three corners; their spacing d = a/√3 is smaller again, so they diffract X-rays at different angles than the (100) or (110) planes.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Lattice constant a = 1 world unit; atoms sit at integer coordinates x,y,z ∈ {-1, 0, 1}, so the cube spans ±1 (2×2×2 world units overall) and is centred on the origin. Sphere radius ≈ 0.10 (about 1/10 of the edge), highlighted in-plane spheres radius ≈ 0.13. Wireframe: black (#1a1a1a) lines of ~1.5 px joining nearest neighbours along all three axes; outer 12 cube edges ~2 px. Colours read from source: spheres bright vermilion #E8332A with a darker maroon rim (#8f1f18) and a small white specular dot upper-left; interior (occluded) portion of the plane deep teal #4E9E95 at ~0.65 opacity; the portion emerging past the top/near faces pale teal #CFE7E3 at ~0.35 opacity — emulate with double-sided material plus depth-based tint, not two separate meshes. Background white. Camera: three-quarter view from slightly above and to the left, the classic textbook cube pose — front-left vertical face nearly facing the viewer, right face receding, top face visible; mild perspective (fov ≈ 30°) so the far edges converge only slightly. Plane geometry: for Miller indices (hkl) the plane is n·r = m·d with unit normal n = (h,k,l)/|(h,k,l)|, d = a/√(h²+k²+l²), m = planeIndex. (100): normal +X, a vertical sheet parallel to the left/right cube faces, passing through x = planeIndex — this matches the LEFT panel of the source, where the sheet sits in the mid-plane through the central column of atoms. (110): normal (1,1,0)/√2, a vertical sheet tilted 45° that cuts from the lower-left front edge up to the upper-right back edge — this matches the RIGHT panel's diagonal slice. (111): normal (1,1,1)/√3, a triangular/hexagonal cut across three corners. Clip each plane to the cube: render it as the convex polygon of intersection with the cube slightly oversized (×1.08) so a thin rim pokes past the faces, as in the source. Labels: Miller index caption and 'd = a/√(h²+k²+l²) = 1.000 a / 0.707 a / 0.577 a' in small dark grey sans-serif below the cube.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the lattice once: InstancedMesh of 27 SphereGeometry(0.10, 24, 16) with MeshStandardMaterial (red, roughness 0.35) and a LineSegments for all nearest-neighbour bonds. Plane: compute the cube–plane intersection polygon analytically (Sutherland–Hodgman clip of a large quad against the 6 cube half-spaces) and rebuild BufferGeometry on family/index change; MeshBasicMaterial with transparent:true, side:DoubleSide, depthWrite:false, and render after the spheres so the teal correctly darkens where it sits behind atoms. For the two-tone look, use a custom shader (or vertex colours along the plane's local up axis) that lerps opacity/colour from deep teal at the lower/interior region to pale teal near the top exit edge. Highlight in-plane atoms by testing |n·p - m·d| < 1e-3 and scaling those instances up with an emissive boost. Clamp planeIndex range per family so the plane always intersects the cube ((100): -1..1, (110): -1..1, (111): -1..1 in units of d, rounded to planes that actually hit atoms). Animate plane translation with a short tween (~250 ms) so the slider reads as sliding through the stack. OrbitControls with damping, no zoom past the cube, target at origin.

authoredContext:
Although the figure depicts a crystal as a two-dimensional array of scattering centers for simplicity, real crystals are structures in three dimensions. Scattering can occur simultaneously from different families of planes at different orientations and spacing patterns known as called Bragg planes, as shown in the figure. The resulting interference pattern can be quite complex.

Because of the regularity that makes a crystal structure, one crystal can have many families of planes within its geometry, each one giving rise to X-ray diffraction.

Figure shows two crystal lattices, with atoms shown as small circles, connected to each other by lines. In the first lattice, flat planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In the second, slanted planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In each case, the planes are seen as a combination of different atoms in the same lattice.

discrepancies: Source shows the two panels' teal sheets as a single uniform mid-tone slab (plus a pale back-face sheet); the generated sheet uses a strong vertical dark→pale gradient and reads as noticeably paler/smaller than the prominent teal square in the source's left panel.
In the source every sphere is identical red; the generated figure enlarges (1.3×) and recolours the in-plane atoms to orange-red, changing the look of the lattice relative to the original.
Initial camera is rotated further (az ≈ 35°, elev ≈ 18°) than the source's near-front, gently-oblique view, so the cube's front face is no longer close to face-on as in the figure.
The two captions sit right on top of the bottom rows of atoms/bonds and are small, partially obscured by the lattice (the d-formula line is hard to read in the render).

Source presents both panels side-by-side for direct comparison; the generated version only ever shows one cube (family toggled), losing the at-a-glance contrast between face-parallel and diagonal planes.
evaluation.notes: A correct, genuinely 3D simple-cubic lattice with real clipped cutting planes and an excellent set of interactions (Miller-family buttons, plane-index slider, stack toggle, guided tour), but the teal sheet reads paler/less dominant than the source, the recoloured/enlarged in-plane atoms depart from the uniform red of the original, and captions are small and collide with the lattice.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct (concept 5, interactivity 5); remaining issues are implementation details—sheet shading/opacity, atom color/size uniformity, initial camera angle, and caption placement/size—that the generator can fix directly.

The source is a two-panel side-by-side comparison (face-parallel vs diagonal cut); the generated version shows only one cube at a time behind family buttons — the direct visual comparison of the two cuts is lost even though both cases are reachable.

Source camera is a shallow axonometric view where the front face reads nearly square; the generated view is rotated further (az 35°, elev 18°) with perspective foreshortening, so the cube looks less like the source's near-orthographic block.
Source has no text annotations; the generated figure adds a caption and a d-spacing formula label at the bottom that slightly overlaps a front-bottom atom.

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two identical cubic crystal lattices drawn side by side in perspective. Each is a three-by-three-by-three array of small red spheres standing for atoms, joined by thin black lines tracing the cube edges and the rows between nearest neighbors, so the block reads as open and transparent. In the left lattice, a translucent teal plane lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the middle sheet of atoms, appearing darker where it sits behind the front layer of spheres and paler where it emerges near the top face. In the right lattice, the highlighted plane is tilted instead, slicing diagonally from the lower left of the cube toward the upper right and intersecting a different set of spheres, its shading again splitting between a darker interior portion and a lighter one near the top. Holding the lattice fixed while changing only the orientation of the shaded plane makes that orientation the single variable in view. The pair conveys that one crystal holds many families of parallel atomic planes at differing angles and spacings, each able to produce its own X-ray diffraction.

elements: 27 small red spheres arranged as a 3x3x3 simple-cubic lattice (atoms), each with a dark red rim/specular highlight
thin black straight lines joining every pair of nearest-neighbour spheres along the three cube axes (3 sheets x 3 lines in each of x, y, z), forming the open wireframe grid
outer cube edges of the lattice, drawn slightly heavier than interior rows
one translucent teal plane cutting through the lattice, rendered double-sided
darker teal region of the plane where it lies behind the front layer of spheres, paler teal where it emerges past the top/side faces (depth-dependent shading)
the sub-set of red spheres that actually lie in the highlighted plane, drawn emphasised (slightly larger / brighter) so the learner sees which atoms the plane contains
Miller-index caption for the current plane family, e.g. (100), (110), (111)
interplanar spacing label d = a / sqrt(h^2+k^2+l^2) with its numeric value
faint ghost outlines of the other parallel planes of the same family, so the family reads as a stack

interactions.teaches: The teal sheet is a genuine 2D plane threading a 3D lattice, not a painted rectangle; rotating shows which atoms really lie in it and how the plane edge-on becomes a line of atoms.

interactions.label: Plane family (Miller indices)
interactions.teaches: One and the same crystal contains several families of parallel atomic planes at different angles; only the plane orientation changes while the red-sphere lattice stays fixed.

interactions.label: Which plane in the stack
interactions.teaches: Stepping to the next parallel plane of the family shifts the sheet by exactly the interplanar spacing d and highlights a different sheet of atoms — the d that enters Bragg's law.

interactions.label: Show whole parallel stack
interactions.teaches: The family is an evenly spaced stack: every atom in the crystal lies on some plane of the family, and the spacing shrinks as the Miller indices grow.

demo_steps.title: Left panel: planes parallel to a cube face
demo_steps.narration: The teal sheet lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the central sheet of nine atoms. This is the (100) family, spacing d = a.

demo_steps.title: Step to the neighbouring plane
demo_steps.narration: Sliding to the next plane translates the sheet by one lattice constant and lights up the front layer of atoms instead — successive planes of the same family are separated by d.

demo_steps.title: The whole (100) stack
demo_steps.narration: Showing all three planes at once reveals that every atom in the crystal belongs to one plane of this evenly spaced family.

demo_steps.title: Right panel: diagonal (110) planes
demo_steps.narration: Now the same lattice is cut diagonally from the lower left toward the upper right. A different set of spheres lies in the plane, and the spacing tightens to d = a/√2.

demo_steps.title: A steeper family still
demo_steps.narration: The (111) planes slice across three corners; their spacing d = a/√3 is smaller again, so they diffract X-rays at different angles than the (100) or (110) planes.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Lattice constant a = 1 world unit; atoms sit at integer coordinates x,y,z ∈ {-1, 0, 1}, so the cube spans ±1 (2×2×2 world units overall) and is centred on the origin. Sphere radius ≈ 0.10 (about 1/10 of the edge), highlighted in-plane spheres radius ≈ 0.13. Wireframe: black (#1a1a1a) lines of ~1.5 px joining nearest neighbours along all three axes; outer 12 cube edges ~2 px. Colours read from source: spheres bright vermilion #E8332A with a darker maroon rim (#8f1f18) and a small white specular dot upper-left; interior (occluded) portion of the plane deep teal #4E9E95 at ~0.65 opacity; the portion emerging past the top/near faces pale teal #CFE7E3 at ~0.35 opacity — emulate with double-sided material plus depth-based tint, not two separate meshes. Background white. Camera: three-quarter view from slightly above and to the left, the classic textbook cube pose — front-left vertical face nearly facing the viewer, right face receding, top face visible; mild perspective (fov ≈ 30°) so the far edges converge only slightly. Plane geometry: for Miller indices (hkl) the plane is n·r = m·d with unit normal n = (h,k,l)/|(h,k,l)|, d = a/√(h²+k²+l²), m = planeIndex. (100): normal +X, a vertical sheet parallel to the left/right cube faces, passing through x = planeIndex — this matches the LEFT panel of the source, where the sheet sits in the mid-plane through the central column of atoms. (110): normal (1,1,0)/√2, a vertical sheet tilted 45° that cuts from the lower-left front edge up to the upper-right back edge — this matches the RIGHT panel's diagonal slice. (111): normal (1,1,1)/√3, a triangular/hexagonal cut across three corners. Clip each plane to the cube: render it as the convex polygon of intersection with the cube slightly oversized (×1.08) so a thin rim pokes past the faces, as in the source. Labels: Miller index caption and 'd = a/√(h²+k²+l²) = 1.000 a / 0.707 a / 0.577 a' in small dark grey sans-serif below the cube.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the lattice once: InstancedMesh of 27 SphereGeometry(0.10, 24, 16) with MeshStandardMaterial (red, roughness 0.35) and a LineSegments for all nearest-neighbour bonds. Plane: compute the cube–plane intersection polygon analytically (Sutherland–Hodgman clip of a large quad against the 6 cube half-spaces) and rebuild BufferGeometry on family/index change; MeshBasicMaterial with transparent:true, side:DoubleSide, depthWrite:false, and render after the spheres so the teal correctly darkens where it sits behind atoms. For the two-tone look, use a custom shader (or vertex colours along the plane's local up axis) that lerps opacity/colour from deep teal at the lower/interior region to pale teal near the top exit edge. Highlight in-plane atoms by testing |n·p - m·d| < 1e-3 and scaling those instances up with an emissive boost. Clamp planeIndex range per family so the plane always intersects the cube ((100): -1..1, (110): -1..1, (111): -1..1 in units of d, rounded to planes that actually hit atoms). Animate plane translation with a short tween (~250 ms) so the slider reads as sliding through the stack. OrbitControls with damping, no zoom past the cube, target at origin.

discrepancies: Camera/projection differs: the source is an almost front-on oblique/axonometric view where each cube's front face reads as a square with depth edges receding up-right; the generated view uses a ~27° perspective that rotates both cubes noticeably and, because the two panels are separated along a view-oblique direction, the right cube is seen at a visibly different angle/scale than the left one (the source shows two identically posed cubes side by side).

Atom colour: in the source every sphere is a saturated red (rear ones only slightly darkened by the teal glass); in the render many interior atoms read as dark grey/near-black spheres, losing the uniform red lattice appearance.
In-plane atoms are enlarged (scale 1.30) and given teal rims — not present in the source, where all 27 spheres are identical in size and colour; useful pedagogically but it alters the look.

The teal sheets extend further beyond the cube faces than in the source (especially the right-hand diagonal plane, which juts well past the lower-left and upper-right corners), making the planes visually dominate more than in the original.

The source's right-hand diagonal plane clearly emerges from the top-left and bottom-right of the cube with a small pale overhang; the generated diagonal plane's orientation/overhang is larger and less tightly clipped to the cube, weakening the 'same cube, different cut' comparison.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and pedagogically rich reconstruction of the two-cube lattice-plane figure with excellent interactions (Miller family buttons, plane-index slider, stack toggle, guided tour), let down mainly by a more rotated perspective view than the source's near-front-on oblique pose, oversized plane overhangs, and interior atoms rendering dark grey rather than red.
action_items: Set the home view closer to the source's front-on oblique pose (small azimuth ~15–20°, small elevation) or use orthographic projection so both cubes are posed identically and their front faces read as squares.
Raise ambient/fill lighting or reduce the plane's opacity/darkening so atoms behind the teal sheet stay clearly red instead of appearing grey-black.
Tighten the plane clipping (reduce CLIP_L) so the pale teal sheet only just emerges past the cube faces, matching the modest overhang in the source.
Consider making the in-plane highlight subtler (teal rim only, no 1.30 scale-up) so the default state matches the source's uniform sphere sizes, with the enlargement reserved for an optional toggle.
plan_action_items: Specify orthographic/axonometric projection and identical per-panel posing (separate panels along the screen-horizontal axis) so the two cubes appear as the same crystal viewed the same way, as in the source.
